bib.title: GIT: A Generative Image-to-text Transformer for Vision and Language

legacy_report:
SOURCE: GIT: A Generative Image-to-text Transformer for Vision and Language. Jianfeng Wang, Zhengyuan Yang, Xiaowei Hu, Linjie Li, Kevin Lin, Zhe Gan, Zicheng Liu, Ce Liu, Lijuan Wang (Microsoft). arXiv 2205.14100v5, dated 15 Dec 2022. The extracted text names no venue, so I am treating it as a preprint.

COVERAGE: I read all 135,884 of 135,884 chars (49 pages): main text, appendices A–G (setting, data loader, captioning, VQA, video, classification, scene text recognition, scaling, cross-attention ablation, decoder and encoder initialisation, intermediate fine-tuning, bias, scene text in pre-training data) and every results table. I skimmed the references. The figure pages are qualitative examples only.

ARCHITECTURE (p3–5, Fig. 2–3):
- One image encoder plus one text decoder. The only objective is the language-modelling (LM) loss.
- Encoder: contrastively pre-trained Florence/CoSwin. Its 2D feature map is flattened, then passed through a linear layer and a layernorm to D=768.
- The image tokens are concatenated with the text embeddings and fed to a 6-block transformer decoder that is randomly initialised. They are not fused by cross-attention.
- Attention mask is seq2seq: image tokens attend to each other, and each text token attends to all image tokens plus the text tokens before it.
- VQA: the question is the caption prefix, and the loss covers only the answer and [EOS].
- Video: 6 frames, each encoded independently, plus a learnable temporal embedding initialised to zero, then concatenated.
- No object detector, no tags, no OCR engine, no pointer network.

CLAIMS
- claim: GIT beats the human score on TextCaps. The "human" number is the human row reported by Sidorov et al. (2020), scored on the test server with automatic metrics. GIT did not take part in any human evaluation.
  number: 138.2 vs 125.5 CIDEr
  setup: GIT (0.7B params, 0.8B pairs), TextCaps test set, server-evaluated, no SCST
  quote: "our model surpasses the human performance for the ﬁrst time on TextCaps (138.2 vs. 125.5 in CIDEr)"; Table 15 caption: "Human: Sidorov et al. (2020)"; test row "Human - - - - - 24.4 26.1 47.0 18.8 125.5" vs "GIT ... 33.1 26.2 52.2 19.6 138.2"
  where: abstract p1; Table 15 p22
- claim: GIT beats the previous TextCaps SOTA (TAP, which uses an OCR engine) by a wide margin. GIT2 goes further.
  number: +28.5 CIDEr; GIT2 145.0
  setup: TextCaps test; TAP# was the CVPR 2021 challenge winner at 109.7
  quote: "our solution outperforms the previous SOTA (TAP Yang et al. (2021c)) by a breakthrough margin (28.5 points in CIDEr)"; "GIT2 38.4 28.3 54.6 21.9 148.6 33.8 27.0 53.0 20.2 145.0"
  where: p6; Table 15 p22
- claim: The model learns to read scene text from the LM loss alone, with no OCR engine. The authors credit the pre-training captions, which often transcribe the text in the image.
  number: 15% of CC12M, 31% of web images
  setup: estimated by running the Azure OCR API over all of CC12M and over 500K web images. A pair counts as a match only if its caption contains an OCR string longer than 5 characters.
  quote: "our approach depends on no OCR engine, and thus no dynamic pointer network. Empirically, we ﬁnd the model gradually learns how to read the scene text with large-scale pre-training"; "It is estimated that 15% of CC12M and 31% of the downloaded images contain scene text descriptions."
  where: p5–6; p11
- claim: Scene text recognition works as captioning. The TextCaps captioner scores 89.9 without any OCR training. Fine-tuned on synthetic OCR data it scores 92.9, which is below MaskOCR's 93.8.
  number: 89.9 / 92.9 / prior 91.9
  setup: average over IC13, SVT, IIIT, IC15, SVTP and CUTE80. For the TextCaps model, a prediction counts if the caption contains the word. For the MJ+ST model it must be an exact match.
  quote: "Our TextCaps-ﬁne-tuned captioning model achieves an 89.9 accuracy ... After ﬁne-tuning the model on the standard MJ+ST datasets, GIT achieves 92.9 that surpasses the prior arts (Fang et al., 2021a; He et al., 2022b) of 91.9."
  where: p10; Table 8 and Table 24 p36 (GIT2 MJ+ST 94.5; GIT "CUTE ... 96.2")
- claim: Text-heavy VQA reaches SOTA or ties it with no OCR input.
  number: ST-VQA 69.6 ANLS (ties LaTr); OCR-VQA 68.1; TextVQA 59.75; VizWiz-QA 67.5
  setup: preceded by intermediate fine-tuning on a mix of VQA datasets, with test and validation images de-duplicated out of that mix
  quote: "we achieve new SOTA on VizWiz-VQA and OCR-VQA, and same performance with prior SOTA of LaTr (Biten et al., 2022) on ST-VQA. Compared with ... Flamingo ... we achieve higher accuracy (+5.4) on TextVQA and lower (-3.29) on VQAv2. Note that Flamingo’s model size is 80B, which is 114 times of ours (0.7B)."
  where: p7; Table 4
- claim: Scaling the image encoder helps, but scaling the text decoder does not. A 6-layer decoder matches or beats 12- and 24-layer ones.
  number: COCO CIDEr 136.4 / 136.0 / 134.6 for 6 / 12 / 24 layers
  setup: pre-trained on a 0.4B-pair subset, no beam search, no SCST
  quote: "Empirically, we ﬁnd it is diﬃcult to eﬀectively scale up the text decoder. Preliminary results are shown in Table 10, which shows a larger decoder shows no improvement."; "6 38.9 30.7 136.4 ... 24 39.1 30.2 134.6"
  where: p11, Table 10
- claim: The authors contrast their decoder-scaling result with Flamingo, whose decoder is pre-trained and frozen.
  number: none
  setup: architectural comparison
  quote: "Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) shows a larger decoder improves the performance. However, their decoder is pre-trained and frozen during the VL pre-training, which avoids the problem of how to eﬀectively train the decoder."; "their decoder is pre-trained and frozen to preserve the generalization capability of the large language model. In our GIT, all parameters are updated"
  where: p5, p11
- claim: Initialising the decoder from BERT gives no gain and sometimes hurts.
  number: Base, random vs BERT-B: COCO 127.5 vs 126.9; TextCaps 61.7 vs 59.7
  setup: GIT_B setup, 10M pairs, learnable weights. The authors say this may not apply to frozen decoders.
  quote: "the text corpus pretrained checkpoint shows no or even worse improvement than the random initialization in both Base and Large sizes"; "may not be applicable to the case with frozen parameters, where the initial weight is important"
  where: Table 26, p37
- claim: Concatenation with self-attention beats a cross-attention decoder at scale, and loses at small scale.
  number: 0.8B pairs, TextCaps: 143.7 without cross-attention vs 139.3 with; 10M pairs, nocaps: 75.4 vs 86.2
  setup: no SCST, no intermediate fine-tuning
  quote: "With smaller dataset, the latter with cross-attention outperforms, while with large-scale data, the former wins."
  where: Table 25, p36
- claim: Contrastive (CLIP) encoder initialisation clearly beats supervised, MAE and random initialisation.
  number: TextCaps 64.9 / 47.0 / 44.9 / 36.5
  setup: GIT_B, ViT-B, 10M pairs. The encoders were pre-trained on different datasets, which confounds the comparison.
  quote: "CLIP 131.4 64.9 61.2 / Supervised 122.1 47.0 58.3 / self-supervised 123.4 44.9 51.6 / Random 89.0 36.5 38.1"
  where: Table 27, p38
- claim: More data and larger encoders help on TextCaps and VizWiz-QA. On COCO and VQAv2 the 0.8B noisy web data helps little or even hurts.
  number: none quotable; the scaling results are only plotted (Fig. 4, Fig. 21)
  setup: Base = CLIP ViT-B/16, Large = ViT-L/14, Huge = CoSwin, each at 4M, 14M and 0.8B images
  quote: "On COCO, the base model beneﬁts from 4M to 14M, but the performance drops with 0.8B data."; "On TextCaps and VizWiz-QA, all model variants beneﬁt signiﬁcantly from more pre-training data. Also, a larger backbone improves more especially with 0.8B data."
  where: p10
- claim: Model and data sizes. GIT2 is 5.1B params, of which 4.8B is the encoder, trained on 10.5B images.
  number: see table
  quote: "GITB 4M 10M CLIP/ViT-B/16 ... 30 129M 224 / GITL 14M 20M CLIP/ViT-L/14 ... 30 347M 224 / GIT 0.8B 0.8B Florence/CoSwin ... 2 681M 384 / GIT2 10.5B 12.9B DaViT ... (4.8B) 2 5.1B 384"; "The text decoder is enlarged to 0.3B"
  where: Table 11, p13
- claim: Pre-training settings.
  number: lr 1e-5 (encoder) and 5e-5 (decoder); batch 4096; 2 epochs; label smoothing 0.1; beam 4
  quote: "The learning rates of the image encoder and the decoder are1e−5 and 5e−5 ... The total number of epochs is2. During inference, the beam size is4"; "The batch size is 4096"
  where: p6, p12
- claim: GIT reaches COCO SOTA on the test server but not on Karpathy test, where OFA scores higher.
  number: COCO test c40 148.8; Karpathy 144.8 vs OFA 145.3; nocaps 123.4 vs CoCa 120.6 (0.7B vs 2.1B)
  quote: "our model achieves the new SOTA performance on all these metrics except on COCO Karpathy test"
  where: p6, Table 2
- claim: Generative VQA and classification trail discriminative models that use the same encoder.
  number: VQAv2 78.81 (1.5 points below Florence); ImageNet 88.79 top-1 (about 1.2 points below Florence)
  quote: "our model performs worse in 1.5 points than the discriminative model of Florence"; "each correct answer requires at least two correct predictions (answer and[EOS]; 2.2 on average)"
  where: p7–8
- claim: Video works by concatenating frames. Example: VATEX private test.
  number: 93.8 vs Flamingo 84.2
  quote: "This is also better than Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022) (84.2) with 80B parameters."
  where: p8

LIMITS:
- No seeds, no variance and no error bars anywhere. Every figure is a single run.
- Of the 0.8B training pairs, 0.6B are a non-public crawl: "an extra 0.6B data following a similar collection procedure in Hu et al. (2021a)". The Florence encoder and the GIT2 data (10.5B images) are also in-house.
- Compute is not quantified. The only statement is A100s on Azure, plus "the number of epoch is only 2 due to computational resource limitation".
- What the authors concede:
  - "it is unclear on how to control the generated caption and how to perform in-context learning without parameter update".
  - Toxic language in the pre-training data "may poison the output".
  - Below discriminative models on VQAv2 and ImageNet.
  - Below Flamingo on MSRVTT-QA (43.2 vs 47.4) and below prior SOTA on TVC.
  - They could not make a larger decoder pay off.
- The "human performance" claim compares CIDEr against human captions scored on the same metric, using a human row taken from Sidorov et al. 2020 (nocaps human row from Agrawal et al. 2019). It is not a human preference study.
- The scene-text prevalence figure is an OCR-API estimate on a subset.
- The bias study (gender and skin NPD of 0.7–5.3%) covers only COCO Karpathy test images annotated by Zhao et al. 2021.
- My own comment, not the authors': the decoder-scaling and random-initialisation findings predate the frozen-LLM-plus-projector lineage (BLIP-2, LLaVA). The authors fence them off explicitly as "not applicable to the case with frozen parameters".

BUILDS ON:
- Florence (Yuan et al., 2021) as encoder and contrastive pre-training; CLIP (Radford et al., 2021); ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021).
- ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021); DaViT (Ding et al., 2022) and UniCL (Yang et al., 2022a) for GIT2.
- Data collection procedure from LEMON (Hu et al., 2021a).
- Random decoder initialisation motivated by MiniVLM (Wang et al., 2020).
- Unified generative VL predecessors: VL-T5 (Cho et al., 2021), SimVLM (Wang et al., 2021b), OFA (Wang et al., 2022b).
- Concurrent work contrasted: CoCa (Yu et al., 2022) and Flamingo (Alayrac et al., 2022).
- OCR-pipeline baselines: M4C (Hu et al., 2020), TAP (Yang et al., 2021c).
- Others: SCST (Rennie et al., 2017); preprocessing from UFO (Wang et al., 2021a); trie-constrained decoding from Wang et al. (2022b); code built on VirTex (Desai & Johnson, 2021).

CODE:
- p8 footnote 3, the exact-match rule for classification: `pred.replace(‘ ’, ‘’) == gt.replace(‘ ’, ‘’)`
- Eq. 1, p5, as extracted (garbled): "l = 1N + 1 N +1∑ i=1 CE(yi,p (yi|I,{yj,j = 0,··· ,i− 1)}), (1) where CE is the cross-entropy loss with label smoothing of 0.1". This is the mean cross-entropy over the N+1 tokens, each conditioned on the image and the tokens before it.

FIGURES:
- Fig. 2 (p4), "Network architecture of our GIT, composed of one image encoder and one text decoder": captioning, VQA-as-prefix and video frames on one page. This is the clearest picture of fusion by concatenation.
- Fig. 3 (p5), "seq2seq attention mask": a 0/1 grid showing image tokens attending each other while text is causal. It explains the mask faster than prose.
- Fig. 4 (p11), "Performance with different pre-training data scales and different model sizes": the encoder-scale-by-data curves on COCO, TextCaps and VizWiz-QA, including the Base-model drop on COCO.
- Fig. 22 (p40): scene text recognition output from the TextCaps captioner set against the MJ+ST model. Useful for the document-understanding note's point about OCR without an OCR engine.
- Fig. 23 (p41): pre-training captions that transcribe scene text. This is the claimed source of the reading ability.

PROBLEMS:
- Equation 1 and the ligatures ("ﬁ", "ﬀ") extract garbled.
- Some table rows merge across columns, e.g. "Open Flamingo (80B, 2.3B) 82.1GIT (0.7B, 0.8B) 78.81" and "GIT TextCaps 89.9MJ+ST 92.9".
- Scaling figures are plots only, so no per-point numbers can be quoted.
